footnote_text: The Greek phrase can function as a totality expression, referring to the whole ordered world rather than only the sky above and the soil below.
Greek pneuma can mean wind, breath, or spirit. This draft keeps a meteorological sense in view, but the phrase remains open for further review.
The Greek verb is from ginomai, which often signals becoming or coming into being. This draft keeps that verbal echo in both command and fulfillment.
Greek uses a cardinal expression here, literally 'day one,' rather than the more expected ordinal 'first day.' The wording may mark the opening day as a distinct starting point.
Greek stereoma points to something fixed or made firm. 'Firm span' aims to preserve that sense without defaulting either to the older 'firmament' or to a purely empty 'expanse.'
Greek speaks of the waters being brought into 'one gathering,' which keeps the image of collected water in view more strongly than the smoother phrase 'one place.'
Greek literally refers to gathered formations or collected bodies of water. This draft shortens the phrase for readability while keeping the sense of ordered water-masses.
The Greek command uses both 'kind' and 'likeness.' This draft keeps both terms visible because the pair may mark both reproductive grouping and recognizable form.
Greek does not simply say 'lights' here but uses a term for bodies that bear or give light. The wording points to heavenly lamps rather than to light as an abstract thing.
Greek uses a noun built from the rule-family rather than a plain verb. 'Dominion' keeps that governing sense visible in the line.
The Greek phrase can cover more than reptiles in a narrow sense. This draft uses 'swarming' to keep the image broad and active.
The Greek keeps both 'image' and 'likeness' rather than using only one term. This draft preserves the pair and leaves their exact relation open for later study.
The Greek verb is stronger than a gentle 'manage.' This wording keeps the force of bringing the earth under ordered human rule.
Greek literally speaks of what has within itself the breath or life-principle of living existence. This draft keeps that animating sense in view.
Greek adds an intensifier, not merely 'good.' The line presents the completed whole as fully and emphatically good.
Greek kosmos can mean an ordered arrangement or adornment, not only 'world' in a modern sense. This draft keeps the idea of a completed, ordered whole.
The Greek here says God completed his works on the sixth day and rested on the seventh. This differs from forms of the text that read 'seventh day' in the first clause.
The Greek closes with an unusual phrase, literally speaking of the works God 'began to make.' This draft keeps that odd ending visible rather than smoothing it away.
Greek literally says 'book of genesis' or 'book of becoming.' This draft keeps the heading's own wordplay visible rather than replacing it with a generic title.
Greek pege usually points to a spring or water source. This draft does not use 'mist' because the verse describes water rising and watering the ground.
The Greek verb suggests shaping or molding, not merely making in a general sense. The line narrows creation imagery from broad making to formed craftsmanship.
Greek paradeisos can denote a planted park or enclosed pleasure-garden. 'Garden' stays readable while leaving room for a fuller note later.
